label: RB1100AHx4 Dude Edition
description: MikroTik RB1100AHx4 Dude Edition (RB1100Dx4) — 13x 1G RJ45. ARM 32bit 4-core AL21400.
notes: Power method from two MikroTik sources, read 2026-11-28, and they name the port. `https://mikrotik.com/product/RB1100Dx4` (HTTP 200, product spec table) prints **Number of AC inputs 2**, **Number of DC inputs 2 (PoE-IN, 2-pin terminal)**, **2-pin terminal input Voltage -48, 20-57 V**, **PoE in 802.3af/at**, **PoE in input Voltage 20-57 V**, **Max power consumption 33 W**, **Max power consumption without attachments 25 W**. `https://help.mikrotik.com/docs/spaces/UM/pages/19136539/RB1100-series` (HTTP 200, the RB1100-series hardware manual) is the one that names the socket: "The device accepts powering from the dual/failover IEC power connectors on the back of the case ... The device also accepts 12-57V passive or 802.3af/at PoE on Ethernet port 13", and under *Extension slots and ports*: "ETH13 port accepts PoE power, and can be used to boot the device from the network". So exactly one of the thirteen copper ports is an inlet - `eth13`, at the 802.3at Type 2 ceiling of 25.5 W - and the other twelve are `poeIn: false`. Every MikroTik row in this catalogue whose sheet states a method but not a port records the inlet on `eth1`; this one is not that case, so the manual's port number is used. `isPoePd()` matched the device-wide `poe-pd` capability and put 12.95 W on all thirteen sockets - **168.35 W** of demand on a box whose own maximum draw is 33 W, and twelve cables asked to power a router that only ever hears about power down the thirteenth.
